phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-046.prompt: A 120-employee private manufacturer has no federal contracts. Finance wants to skip the EEO-1 because 'that form is only for contractors.' What should the PHR advise?

options.a: File Component 1; private employers with 100 or more employees report workforce demographics to the EEOC
options.b: Skip the filing; EEO-1 Component 1 applies only to federal contractors with 50 or more employees
options.c: File VETS-4212 instead; that veterans report replaced EEO-1 for private non-contractor employers
options.d: Submit last year's affirmative action plan to OFCCP and treat that contractor packet as the EEO-1 filing

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-046.explanation: EEO-1 Component 1 is a workforce demographic report to the EEOC. Private employers with 100 or more employees generally must file, even with no federal contract. The contractor threshold (often 50 employees plus a qualifying contract) is an additional coverage path, not the only one. VETS-4212 and AAPs are separate contractor obligations.

distractorExplanations.b: Contractor coverage is extra, not exclusive; a 100-employee private firm typically still files Component 1.
distractorExplanations.c: VETS-4212 is a veterans employment report for certain contractors; it did not replace the EEO-1.
distractorExplanations.d: An AAP is an OFCCP contractor document, not a substitute EEO-1 Component 1 filing with the EEOC.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-047.prompt: A new operations VP wants last year's EEO-1 uploaded into the OFCCP audit folder and labeled 'our AAP.' What should HR explain?

options.a: The EEO-1 is the AAP; attaching the prior-year Component 1 filing satisfies an OFCCP audit
options.b: The EEO-1 is an EEOC demographic snapshot; an AAP is a separate contractor planning document
options.c: OFCCP treats Component 1 job-category counts as a complete utilization analysis with goals
options.d: Only EEO-1 pay-data Component 2, when collected, functions as the written affirmative action plan

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-047.explanation: The EEO-1 tells the EEOC how the workforce looks by job category, sex, and race/ethnicity at a snapshot. An affirmative action plan for covered federal contractors is a different OFCCP document with utilization, goals, and outreach analysis. Re-labeling an EEO-1 as an AAP leaves the contractor file incomplete.

distractorExplanations.a: Component 1 is not an AAP; OFCCP expects a distinct plan, not a recycled EEOC headcount file.
distractorExplanations.c: Job-category counts on the EEO-1 are not a utilization analysis with incumbency versus availability.
distractorExplanations.d: Pay-data collection, when it occurs, still is not the narrative AAP contractors must maintain.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-048.prompt: Payroll offers W-2 totals, home addresses, and SSNs 'to make the EEO-1 more useful to the government.' What belongs on Component 1?

options.a: Each employee's exact wages and bonus so the EEOC can run a pay-equity audit
options.b: Only the top-five executives' demographics, because they represent the employer
options.c: Headcount by EEO job category, sex, and race/ethnicity for the snapshot period
options.d: Home addresses and SSNs so the EEOC can match employees to census files

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-048.explanation: Component 1 is a demographic headcount: employees grouped into EEO job categories with sex and race/ethnicity counts for a selected pay period. It is not a dump of SSNs, home addresses, or individual W-2 amounts. Mixing identifiers into the EEO-1 workpapers also creates a privacy incident without helping the filing.

distractorExplanations.a: Individual wage lines are not what Component 1 collects; that confuses the form with a pay study.
distractorExplanations.b: The report covers the workforce in EEO categories, not a handful of named executives.
distractorExplanations.d: SSNs and home addresses are not EEO-1 fields and should not ride along as 'helpful' extras.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-049.prompt: A picker hired four years ago resigned eight months ago. Counsel asks whether that Form I-9 can be shredded this week. What is the retention rule?

options.a: Destroy it now; three years after the hire date already passed last calendar year
options.b: Keep it seven years so I-9 retention matches common employment-tax record habits
options.c: Destroy it the day after the final paycheck because IRCA ends at termination
options.d: Keep it until one year after termination, the later of the two statutory dates

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-049.explanation: Employers retain each I-9 for three years after the hire date or one year after termination, whichever is later. Here three years after hire already passed, but one year after the resignation is still about four months away, so the form stays. Neither IRS seven-year habits nor 'destroy at final pay' replace that later-of rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Three years after hire is only one prong; when termination is later, keep one year after exit.
distractorExplanations.b: Seven years is a tax-file convention, not the IRCA I-9 retention period.
distractorExplanations.c: IRCA does not let you destroy the I-9 at the last paycheck; post-termination time still runs.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-050.prompt: A supervisor tells a new hire to 'just bring a U.S. passport so HR does not have to look at other papers.' What should the PHR do?

options.a: Stop the request; the employee may present any acceptable List A document or List B plus List C
options.b: Allow it if the supervisor puts the passport-only instruction in a written email to HR staff
options.c: Require the passport plus a Social Security card so identity and work status are dual-checked
options.d: Accept only passports for adult hires because List B identity documents are limited to minors

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-050.explanation: Document abuse occurs when an employer specifies which acceptable I-9 documents the employee must show. The employee chooses any valid List A document or a List B identity document plus a List C work-authorization document. A manager's 'passport only' instruction is unlawful even if meant to speed Section 2.

distractorExplanations.b: A written manager preference does not legalize specifying documents; the choice remains the employee's.
distractorExplanations.c: If List A is presented, List C is not required; stacking extra papers is another form of specification.
distractorExplanations.d: List B is not a minor-only list; adults may present List B plus List C instead of List A.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-051.prompt: An LPR presented an unexpired Permanent Resident Card (Form I-551) at hire. Two years later the date printed on the card has passed. Should HR reverify?

options.a: Yes; complete Section 3 within three business days of the printed card date
options.b: Yes, but only if E-Verify previously returned a tentative nonconfirmation
options.c: No; do not reverify an LPR I-551 solely because the card's printed date passed
options.d: Remove the person from the schedule until a newly issued green card is produced

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-051.explanation: USCIS instructions tell employers not to reverify U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents who presented a Form I-551. The card's expiration date does not end LPR status or restart Section 3. Reverification is for temporary work authorization that actually expires, not for a green card date.

distractorExplanations.a: Section 3 timing for expiring temporary work papers does not apply to an I-551 LPR presentation.
distractorExplanations.b: E-Verify TNC history does not create an I-9 reverification duty for an LPR green card.
distractorExplanations.d: Pulling the employee off the schedule treats a card reprint as lost work authorization, which it is not.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-052.prompt: ICE serves a Notice of Inspection for Forms I-9. How should those records have been stored so HR can produce them without over-disclosing?

options.a: Inside each medical file, because identity documents are treated as ADA medical information
options.b: Only as a scanned offer letter in the ATS, which substitutes for Form I-9 in an audit
options.c: In the public OSHA 300 log binder so safety and immigration records travel together
options.d: In a dedicated I-9 file or system, produced without dumping full personnel or medical files

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-052.explanation: Best practice is to keep I-9s (and copies of documents, if you copy) in a separate file or system so an ICE inspection does not become a wholesale personnel-file dump. Medical files, OSHA logs, and ATS offer letters are the wrong homes: they mix legally distinct records and either withhold the actual Form I-9 or over-disclose unrelated data.

distractorExplanations.a: I-9 identity documents are not ADA medical records and do not belong in the confidential medical file.
distractorExplanations.b: An offer letter is not Form I-9; ICE inspects the I-9 itself, not ATS recruiting PDFs.
distractorExplanations.c: OSHA injury logs are posted/workplace safety records, not an immigration audit binder.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-053.prompt: A warehouse employee strains a back lifting a crate, misses two shifts, works restricted duty, and later fills a prescription muscle relaxer. Ice was used on day one. How should OSHA recording be handled?

options.a: Skip the OSHA log because an ice pack is first aid, and first aid keeps the whole case off the log
options.b: Record it on the OSHA 300 log; days away, restriction, or a prescription each make the case recordable
options.c: File only the state workers' compensation first report and skip OSHA forms when WC is involved
options.d: Wait 180 days before recording; OSHA recording begins only after six months of work restriction

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-053.explanation: A work-related case is recordable if it involves death, days away, restricted work or transfer, medical treatment beyond first aid, loss of consciousness, or a significant diagnosed injury. Missed shifts, restricted duty, and a prescription drug each independently meet the test. First-aid ice on day one does not cancel those later criteria, and workers' comp filing is a separate insurance process.

distractorExplanations.a: First aid does not wipe recordability once days away, restriction, or prescription treatment occur.
distractorExplanations.c: A state WC claim form does not replace the OSHA 300/301 recordkeeping duty for covered employers.
distractorExplanations.d: There is no 180-day waiting period; recording is due within seven calendar days of receiving information that a recordable case occurred.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-054.prompt: On February 10 a plant manager asks when the annual injury summary can come down off the break-room board. What is the OSHA 300A posting window?

options.a: Keep Form 300A posted February 1 through April 30 where employee notices are customarily posted
options.b: Post the annual summary only on the day an OSHA compliance officer is expected on the site
options.c: Post each Form 301 incident report on the wall for the full calendar year instead of 300A
options.d: Email 300A to OSHA and skip workplace posting whenever the establishment e-files injury data

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-054.explanation: Covered establishments must post the Form 300A annual summary from February 1 through April 30 in a conspicuous place where workplace notices usually appear. February 10 is still inside that window, so the poster stays up. Electronic submission, if required, does not replace the employee posting, and Form 301 is an incident report, not the annual summary employees must see.

distractorExplanations.b: Inspection-day-only posting defeats the three-month employee notice OSHA requires.
distractorExplanations.c: Form 301 is the case incident report; posting every 301 would also expose more detail than 300A.
distractorExplanations.d: E-file or electronic submission, where it applies, is in addition to—not instead of—the Feb–Apr posting.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-055.prompt: A finger is cleaned, bandaged, and the employee returns to full duty the same shift. No prescription, stitches, or lost time. Is this OSHA-recordable for a covered employer?

options.a: Yes; any visible blood on a tool automatically becomes an OSHA recordable case under Part 1904
options.b: Yes; every workers' compensation claim, even if later denied, must appear on the 300 log
options.c: Yes; adhesive bandages count as medical treatment beyond first aid under OSHA recordkeeping rules
options.d: Generally no; cleaning and a bandage without days away, restriction, or treatment beyond first aid stays first aid

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-055.explanation: OSHA lists cleaning wounds and using bandages as first aid. First aid alone, with no days away, restricted work, job transfer, or medical treatment beyond first aid, is not recordable. Blood on a tool, a WC claim, or a bandage does not by itself convert the case. Contrast this with prescription medication, stitches, or lost time, which typically do.

distractorExplanations.a: Blood exposure on equipment is not an automatic 300-log trigger; apply the recording criteria.
distractorExplanations.b: Workers' comp and OSHA recordkeeping use different tests; a WC filing does not force a 300 entry.
distractorExplanations.c: Bandages are on OSHA's first-aid list, not medical treatment beyond first aid.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-056.prompt: Outside counsel is redlining the employee handbook in an at-will state. Which disclaimer best reduces implied-contract risk?

options.a: Employment is promised for at least 12 months after the employee signs the acknowledgment
options.b: Discipline will follow every numbered step in the progressive-discipline chart in every case
options.c: The handbook is not a contract; employment is at-will and the company may revise policies
options.d: Policies change only when a majority of employees vote to accept the revision

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-056.explanation: Handbooks can create implied contracts if they guarantee tenure or lock the employer into every listed process. A clear at-will statement, a 'not a contract' disclaimer, and a reserved right to change policies are the usual PHR controls. Promising a year of work, promising every discipline step, or requiring an employee vote does the opposite.

distractorExplanations.a: A one-year guarantee is a term contract, which undercuts at-will instead of preserving it.
distractorExplanations.b: Mandatory step charts are a classic implied-contract hook that limits discharge discretion.
distractorExplanations.d: Requiring an employee vote to change rules treats the handbook like a bargained contract.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-057.prompt: Operations wants a 40-page overtime-approval SOP copied into the employee handbook 'so nobody can say they were not told.' What is the better PHR design?

options.a: Keep a short handbook rule and house the detailed SOP in a manager policy you can update
options.b: Paste every operational SOP into the handbook so the acknowledgment covers each procedure
options.c: Replace the handbook with Slack pins, which never create handbook-contract risk
options.d: Publish overtime rules only inside a union contract, even at a nonunion site

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-057.explanation: The handbook is the employee-facing summary of rules and disclaimers. Long manager SOPs belong in a policy/procedure library so operations can revise workflows without implying that every checklist is a contractual right. A receipt acknowledgment still covers the handbook rule. Slack pins are still communications that can create expectations, and a nonunion site has no CBA to hide procedures in.

distractorExplanations.b: Stuffing SOPs into the handbook bloats it and makes each revision look like a bargained term.
distractorExplanations.c: Informal chat posts can still create policy promises; they are not a safe substitute handbook.
distractorExplanations.d: A nonunion employer has no union contract vehicle; that answer invents a CBA that does not exist.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-058.prompt: A supervisor emails the whole shift a scanned doctor's note describing an employee's lifting limits 'so everyone can help.' What should HR do?

options.a: File the doctor's note in the ordinary personnel file so any future supervisor can open it
options.b: Add the diagnosis to the OSHA 300A annual posting so coworkers see why the job was modified
options.c: Forward the doctor's note to payroll to store with Forms I-9, because leave tracking sits with hire forms
options.d: Move it into a confidential medical file, separate from personnel, and limit access to need-to-know

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-058.explanation: ADA (and related privacy practice) requires that employee medical information be collected on a need-to-know basis and kept in a confidential medical file separate from the personnel file. A team-wide email of a doctor's note is a disclosure. Coworkers may need a functional restriction ('no lifts over 20 pounds'), not the diagnosis or the scan.

distractorExplanations.a: The personnel file is too broadly available; medical notes do not belong there.
distractorExplanations.b: The 300A summary is an injury-count poster, not a place to publish a coworker's diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.c: I-9 files are for employment-eligibility forms, not medical notes or FMLA clinical detail.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-059.prompt: Benefits asks HR to email a spreadsheet of employee Social Security numbers to a new broker 'to speed the census.' What is the right privacy response?

options.a: Send the file if the spreadsheet name includes the word confidential
options.b: CC the entire leadership team so executives share responsibility for the transfer
options.c: Refuse the open email; send only needed fields through a secure channel to a vetted vendor
options.d: Post the census on the intranet so employees can self-correct SSNs before the broker sees them

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-059.explanation: SSNs are high-risk personal data. PHR practice is minimum necessary: confirm the broker is under contract, use a secure transfer, and send only the fields the census actually requires. A 'confidential' filename, a wider CC list, or an intranet post increases exposure instead of reducing it and can trigger state breach-notice duties if the file is misdirected.

distractorExplanations.a: A filename label does not encrypt the attachment or stop a misaddressed email from being a breach.
distractorExplanations.b: Copying more executives multiplies inboxes that hold SSNs; it does not transfer legal risk away from HR.
distractorExplanations.d: Posting SSNs internally is a broadcast, not a safeguard, and far exceeds need-to-know.

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-060.prompt: A line manager wants PDFs of every direct report's full personnel file for 'career talks,' including investigation memos and I-9 copies. What should HR release?

options.a: The entire personnel file; any supervisor of record is entitled to every document stored in that file
options.b: Job-related performance documents on a need-to-know basis, not investigations, medical notes, or I-9s
options.c: I-9 copies and medical notes, but withhold performance reviews as too sensitive for line managers
options.d: The full PDFs to the manager's personal email so the files can be read off-network at home

phr-hrci-readiness-check-compliance-060.explanation: Personnel information is disclosed on a need-to-know basis. A supervisor may see current performance, goals, and job history needed to coach. Investigation files, medical information, and I-9s serve other legal purposes and are not career-talk material. Emailing full files to a personal account also loses custody of sensitive records.

distractorExplanations.a: Supervisor status is not a master key to investigations, medical data, or I-9s.
distractorExplanations.c: That pair is backwards: performance is what the manager needs; I-9s and medical notes are not.
distractorExplanations.d: Personal email takes records outside employer systems and heightens a privacy incident.
